title: California Prepares to Celebrate Its First Diwali as an Official State Holiday
excerpt: Assembly Bill 268 makes California the third U.S. state to recognize the festival of lights, giving nearly 900,000 Indian Americans a new marker of cultural inclusion.
body:
• California will celebrate Diwali as an official state holiday for the first time on November 8, 2026, after Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 268 into law in October 2025.
  • The legislation allows public schools and community colleges to close and gives state employees paid time off, though courts will remain open.
  • California becomes the third U.S. state to recognize Diwali after Pennsylvania (2024) and Connecticut (2025), with New York City also observing it as a public school holiday.
  • With nearly 900,000 Indian Americans, California has the largest Indian-origin population of any state, making the recognition a milestone for cultural inclusion.

California is preparing to mark a historic first this fall: the state's inaugural celebration of Diwali as an official state holiday, set for November 8, 2026.

The milestone follows Governor Gavin Newsom's signing of Assembly Bill 268 in October 2025, which added the Hindu festival of lights to California's roster of recognized holidays. Under the state's default rules for new legislation, the law took effect on January 1, 2026, setting the stage for this year's observance.

What the Law Means in Practice

AB 268, authored by Democratic Assemblymembers Ash Kalra of San Jose and Dr. Darshana Patel, gives public schools and community colleges the option to close on Diwali. State employees may take paid time off to observe the holiday. Courts, however, are excluded from judicial holidays and will remain open.

https://x.com/NDTVWorld/status/2090964983060595111

The bill also encourages educational institutions to incorporate activities that acknowledge and celebrate the cultural significance of Diwali, a festival observed by Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, and Jains that symbolizes the triumph of light over darkness.

"Diwali brings communities together with the message of goodwill, peace and shared sense of renewal. California should embrace Diwali and its diversity, not keep it hidden in darkness."

— Ash Kalra, California Assemblymember

Kalra, the first Indian-American legislator in California's history, championed the bill through both chambers of the legislature, where it cleared the Senate on September 10, 2025, and the Assembly the following day.

A Growing Nationwide Trend

California is the third U.S. state to formally recognize Diwali as a holiday. Pennsylvania led the way in 2024, followed by Connecticut, which added Diwali through Public Act 25-59, effective October 1, 2025. New York City separately observes Diwali as a public school holiday. North Carolina has also celebrated the festival as a state observance.

The trend reflects the growing visibility of South Asian communities in American civic life. With a billion people celebrating worldwide, Diwali is among the most widely observed festivals globally and the most important holiday of the year in India.

A Milestone for the Indian Diaspora

California's nearly 900,000 Indian Americans make it the largest Indian-origin population of any U.S. state, and community leaders have hailed the recognition as a long-overdue step toward inclusion.

MR Rangaswami, founder of Indiaspora, a leading nonprofit representing the Indian diaspora, called the law "a major milestone in the ongoing journey toward greater cultural inclusion and visibility." He credited the decision to honoring "generations of Indian Americans who have contributed to California's growth and diversity."

"Governor Newsom's leadership reflects the inclusive spirit our nation needs today. Recognizing Diwali as a state holiday affirms that diversity is truly our strength."

— MR Rangaswami, Founder, Indiaspora

Ajay Bhutoria, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and former advisor to President Joe Biden for the AANHPI Commission, also praised the move, thanking Newsom and the bill's authors on social media.

Gopala Ajjarapu, president of Sri Satyanarayana Swamy Devasthanam, a Hindu temple in Milpitas, told the Mercury News the new law made him "proud and happy," calling it a sign that the U.S., a "country of immigrants," is becoming "even more inclusive."

What to Expect on November 8

This year's Diwali falls on Saturday, November 8. While the holiday's placement on a weekend means the immediate impact on school and government closures will be limited, the symbolic weight of the recognition remains significant. The date moves annually based on the Hindu lunar calendar, falling on the 15th day of Kartik and typically landing in October or November.

In the Bay Area and across the state, large-scale community festivals, temple celebrations, and cultural events are expected to mark the occasion. Celebrants will exchange gifts, light lamps, and gather for prayers in what has become one of the most visible cultural celebrations in California's diverse calendar.

The designation also opens the door for broader workplace recognition, with employee advocates noting that the holiday status gives staff the flexibility to honor Diwali without compromising professional responsibilities. For the rapidly growing Indian American community in California and beyond, the law represents not just a holiday, but a statement about belonging.
